\chapter{Who, and How Many}
\label{ch:mr-who-how-many}
\hlchaptermodality{37}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can ask which person is meant with koṇ and ask for a quantity with kitī, and I can say what shape of answer each of the k- asking words wants.}

Complete MR-R37-who-how-many and sort three asking words by the shape of the answer they demand: a thing, a person, a number.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[koṇ]{\mr{कोण} (koṇ) — who}

\label{lesson:MR-C37-kon}



\begin{quote}
You own one asking word: \textbf{\mr{काय}} (\emph{kāy}), \textbf{what}. It asks about a thing. Nothing you own yet asks about a \textbf{person}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \mr{कोण}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{कोण}} — \emph{koṇ} — \textbf{who}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{तो} \mr{कोण} \mr{आहे}?} — \emph{to koṇ āhe?} — \textbf{who is that?}
\end{quote}

\textbf{\mr{कोण}} asks for a person the way \textbf{\mr{काय}} asks for a thing. Both begin with \textbf{\mr{क}}, and that is not luck: Marathi builds its asking words on one inherited stem. \textbf{\mr{काय}}, \textbf{\mr{कसा}}, \textbf{\mr{कोण}} — the \textbf{\mr{क}-} family. Meet a new word starting with \textbf{\mr{क}} in a question and you can guess its job before you know its meaning.

\textbf{\mr{कोण}} comes down from Sanskrit \textbf{\mr{कः}} (\emph{kaḥ}, \textquotedblleft{}who\textquotedblright{}), by way of the older Marathi \textbf{\mr{कवण}}. English \textbf{who} and Latin \textbf{quis} grew from the same Indo-European stem, which is why the family feels oddly familiar.

Point it at somebody you have already named: \textbf{\mr{मीरा} \mr{कोण} \mr{आहे}?} — \emph{Mīrā koṇ āhe?} — \textbf{who is Mira?}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{koṇ} — who
  \item \emph{mitra koṇ āhe?} — who is the friend?
  \item which letter every Marathi asking word so far begins with — \textbf{\mr{क}}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which word asks for a thing, and which for a person? (\textbf{\mr{काय}}; \textbf{\mr{कोण}}.) What do they share? (\textbf{The \mr{क}- stem}.)

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%A4\%95\%E0\%A5\%8B\%E0\%A4\%A3}{Wiktionary: \mr{कोण}}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[kitī]{\mr{किती} (kitī) — how many}

\label{lesson:MR-C37-kiti}



\begin{quote}
You can count \textbf{\mr{एक} \mr{दोन} \mr{तीन} \mr{चार} \mr{पाच}}. You met \textbf{\mr{कोण}} one lesson ago. Neither of them lets you ask somebody for a number.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \mr{किती}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{किती}} — \emph{kitī} — \textbf{how many, how much}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{तुम्हाला} \mr{किती} \mr{भाऊ} \mr{आहेत}?} — \emph{tumhālā kitī bhāū āhet?} — \textbf{how many brothers do you have?}
\end{quote}

Another \textbf{\mr{क}-} word, and the answer to it is always a number. That is what makes it worth spending a lesson on so early: five numbers with no question to trigger them are five words nobody asks you for.

\textbf{\mr{किती}} is Sanskrit \textbf{\mr{कति}} (\emph{kati}, \textquotedblleft{}how many\textquotedblright{}) barely changed. Latin \textbf{quot} and English \textbf{how many} carry the same ancient stem.

It also does duty for \textbf{how much} of something uncountable — Marathi does not split the two the way English does.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{kitī} — how many
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{kitī bhāū?} — how many brothers?
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{dusrā} — the other one — then answer \emph{kitī?} with \emph{don}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What kind of answer does \textbf{\mr{किती}} always want? (\textbf{A number}.) And \textbf{\mr{कोण}}? (\textbf{A person}.)

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%A4\%95\%E0\%A4\%BF\%E0\%A4\%A4\%E0\%A5\%80}{Wiktionary: \mr{किती}}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[koṇ? · kitī?]{Sort the answers, not the questions}

\label{lesson:MR-R37-who-how-many}



\begin{quote}
Three asking words are now yours. Name them in the order you met them, oldest first.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{kāy āhe?} — and answer with a thing
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{koṇ āhe?} — and answer with a person
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{kitī?} — and answer with a numeral between \emph{ek} and \emph{pāch}
  \item \emph{Recall:} read the form label \textbf{\mr{आवडती} \mr{कृती}} and say why it ends in \textbf{-\mr{ती}}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
All three begin with the same letter. Which? (\textbf{\mr{क}}.) So what does a strange new \textbf{\mr{क}-} word at the front of a sentence probably want from you? (\textbf{An answer} — it is a question.)
\end{tcolorbox}
